item.title: Nvidia's CUDA Faces New Threats from AI Coding Agents in 2026
item.description: AI coding agents are automating GPU kernel development, threatening Nvidia's two-decade CUDA software moat as competitors and cloud giants offer alternatives.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia’s CUDA platform has been the undisputed foundation of AI computing for nearly two decades, but a new threat is emerging that traditional competitors could never mount: AI coding agents that can write, port, and optimize GPU software autonomously. These agents are collapsing the engineering effort required to build CUDA-compatible software stacks, enabling competitors like AMD, cloud giants, and startups to bypass Nvidia’s most formidable competitive advantage — its software moat.

The Two-Decade Moat That Made Nvidia Untouchable

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) launched in 2007 as a way to program Nvidia GPUs for general-purpose computing. Over the following 18 years, Nvidia invested billions of dollars building a software ecosystem that includes compilers, libraries, debuggers, profilers, and deep learning frameworks — all optimized exclusively for Nvidia hardware. By 2026, CUDA represents millions of lines of code and decades of developer workflows that competitors cannot easily replicate.

This software moat has been Nvidia’s most powerful defensive weapon. Even when competitors like AMD produced competitive hardware, the sheer cost of porting existing CUDA code to alternative platforms kept developers locked into the Nvidia ecosystem. Amazon’s internal documents identified CUDA as a major roadblock to adoption of its own Trainium and Inferentia chips, according to Business Insider. The message was clear: no matter how good your hardware, if it doesn’t run CUDA software, developers won’t use it.

The moat was considered so formidable that SemiAnalysis, a respected semiconductor research firm, had long rated AMD’s chances of breaking the CUDA moat at effectively zero. That assessment has now changed dramatically.

AI Coding Agents Are Learning to Write GPU Software

The game-changing development of 2026 is that AI coding agents — tools like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor — have crossed a threshold where they can generate, port, and optimize GPU-level system software. This matters because the hardest part of competing with Nvidia was never building the hardware; it was writing the millions of lines of software that make hardware usable.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng told Business Insider that combining AI coding agents with TileLang, a hardware-agnostic tensor compiler, has made AI software substantially easier to build. Instead of requiring teams of expert CUDA engineers to hand-optimize kernels for each hardware platform, developers can now describe what they want in natural language and let AI agents generate the implementation.

OpenAI and Anthropic have both demonstrated AI models capable of generating system-level software, including GPU kernels. This represents a fundamental shift: the bottleneck is no longer engineering talent but the quality of the AI model and the availability of machine-readable hardware specifications.

Case Study: Infinity Recreates CUDA in 10 Hours

The most striking evidence of this shift comes from Infinity, a startup founded by Jeremy Nixon. In August 2026, Infinity used AI coding agents to recreate CUDA-like software for D-Matrix, an AI chip startup, in just 10 hours. What would have taken a team of expert engineers months or years was accomplished by a small team directing AI agents.

This is not an isolated experiment. In January 2026, Claude Code autonomously ported LeelaChessZero’s CUDA backend to AMD’s ROCm platform, as documented in GitHub PR #2375. The port involved translating complex GPU kernel code from Nvidia’s CUDA dialect to AMD’s HIP (Heterogeneous-Compute Interface for Portability) — a task that previously required deep expertise in both platforms.

These examples demonstrate that AI coding agents have crossed a critical capability threshold. They can now handle the kind of low-level system programming that was previously the exclusive domain of specialized engineers with years of GPU programming experience.

AMD’s Bold Bet — Machine-Readable ISA and ROCm.AI

AMD has seized on this trend with a strategy that directly targets the CUDA moat. At its Advancing AI 2026 event in July, AMD unveiled ROCm.AI, a suite of tools that lets developers use AI coding agents to build and optimize software for AMD Instinct GPUs.

The centerpiece of AMD’s strategy is publishing a machine-readable Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) for its GPUs. This means frontier AI models can program directly to AMD hardware without going through a human-written compiler or translation layer. Instead of the old approach — “write in CUDA, then translate to ROCm” — developers can now say “write for AMD hardware” and let AI agents generate native code.

AMD’s ROCm.AI plugs directly into existing code assistants like Claude Code, providing tools to deploy, debug, and optimize for AMD Instinct hardware. The company also demonstrated Hyperloom, an automated workload optimization system that boosted model performance by 38% over baseline on Helios racks, according to The Register.

Perhaps most significantly, AMD has cultivated close relationships with OpenAI and Anthropic to train frontier models on AMD hardware and software internals. Anthropic’s Head of Compute, Tom Brown, used Claude with the “/goal” command to bring up an inference stack on AMD hardware over a single weekend — a task that would have taken weeks using traditional methods.

SemiAnalysis has now upgraded AMD from a 0% chance to a “great chance of success” at breaking the CUDA moat. Anthropic publicly announced plans to deploy 2GW of AMD’s chips for inference workloads. Microsoft, after previously dropping AMD’s MI300X, has reversed course and is now adopting AMD hardware.

The Inference Shift — Why CUDA Lock-In Weakens

A structural shift in the AI industry is working against Nvidia’s moat: the market is moving from training to inference. During the training phase, organizations demand maximum performance and are willing to pay a premium for Nvidia’s best hardware and software. But inference — the process of running trained models to generate outputs — is a different game entirely.

Marshall Choy of Rebellions, an AI chip startup, told Business Insider: “The CUDA moat gets broken because CUDA is no longer a factor on the inference side.” When companies run AI models in production, they care about cost per query, power efficiency, and total cost of ownership — not peak theoretical performance. This makes alternative platforms with competitive price-performance ratios attractive, even if they require some software migration effort.

The shift from training to inference reduces CUDA’s lock-in advantage because inference workloads are less dependent on the deep software optimization that makes CUDA indispensable for training. Inference frameworks like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM (which now supports multiple backends), and open-source runtimes are increasingly hardware-agnostic.

Chris Lattner, co-founder of Modular and creator of the LLVM compiler infrastructure, described CUDA’s position with a memorable analogy: “CUDA carries legacy tech like Microsoft Windows trying to fit onto a phone.” The implication is clear — CUDA was designed for an era of hand-crafted GPU kernels and gaming graphics, not for an era of AI-generated code and heterogeneous computing.

Cloud Giants and Startups Join the Attack

The assault on CUDA’s dominance is not limited to AMD. Every major cloud provider has spent years building software around their own AI chips, and AI coding agents are accelerating those efforts.

Google has its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) with the XLA compiler stack, which has always been designed for a compiler-driven, hardware-agnostic approach. Google’s investment in JAX, a numerical computing framework that compiles to XLA, means that models written in JAX can target TPUs, GPUs, or CPUs with minimal changes. AI coding agents make it even easier to port JAX workloads between hardware platforms.

Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia chips have struggled with CUDA dependency, but AI coding agents are reducing the cost of porting PyTorch and TensorFlow models to Amazon’s custom silicon. Amazon’s internal documents identified CUDA as a major roadblock, but the company is now investing in AI-powered tooling to automate the migration.

Microsoft, after initially adopting AMD’s MI300X and then dropping it, has reversed course and is now embracing AMD hardware again. The flexibility that AI coding agents provide for software migration makes it less risky for cloud giants to diversify their hardware supply chains.

Startups are also benefiting. Rebellions, D-Matrix, Groq, and Cerebras all have competitive hardware but previously faced the “software problem” — no developer wants to write code for a niche platform. AI coding agents solve this by automating the porting process, dramatically reducing the cost of supporting alternative hardware.

Nvidia’s Paradox — Using AI Agents to Defend CUDA

Nvidia is not standing still. The company itself uses AI coding agents to develop CUDA faster and validate the platform at greater scale than ever before. Nvidia’s internal AI agents help write and test CUDA kernels, optimize library performance, and catch bugs in the massive CUDA codebase.

This creates a paradox: the same AI coding agents that help Nvidia strengthen CUDA also help competitors port away from it. Every improvement in AI coding capabilities benefits both sides of the equation. Nvidia can develop CUDA features faster, but AMD and others can use the same AI tools to build compatible software stacks faster.

Nvidia’s strategy appears to be doubling down on performance leadership. If Nvidia can maintain a meaningful hardware performance advantage, the software moat becomes less critical — developers will use CUDA because Nvidia GPUs are the fastest, not because they’re the only option. But this strategy carries risk: if AI coding agents narrow the software gap faster than Nvidia can widen the hardware gap, the moat erodes from both sides.

What the CUDA Moat’s Erosion Means for the AI Industry

The erosion of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, driven by AI coding agents, has profound implications for the entire AI industry.

More competition, lower costs. When multiple hardware platforms can run AI workloads efficiently, prices come down. The GPU shortage that has plagued AI development since 2023 could ease as organizations gain the flexibility to use AMD, cloud custom chips, and startups’ hardware alongside Nvidia GPUs.

Faster innovation in hardware. A world where software portability is automated means hardware startups can focus on building better chips instead of building software ecosystems. This could accelerate the pace of hardware innovation as more companies enter the market.

Open-source software stacks gain ground. AMD’s decision to open-source its compiler and kernels positions it well for the agentic age. When AI agents can read source code and generate compatible implementations, open-source platforms have a structural advantage over proprietary ones.

Nvidia remains dominant — for now. Despite the threats, Nvidia still holds commanding advantages: the best hardware performance, the most mature software ecosystem, and the deepest relationships with AI researchers. The CUDA moat is eroding, not collapsing. But the direction of travel is clear, and the pace of change is accelerating.

The agentic era favors flexibility. The companies that will thrive in the coming years are those that embrace AI coding agents as a core part of their strategy. AMD’s machine-readable ISA and ROCm.AI represent a bet that the future belongs to platforms designed for AI agents, not for human programmers. If that bet pays off, the CUDA era — one of the most remarkable runs in technology history — may be entering its final chapter.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the CUDA moat and why does it matter?

The CUDA moat refers to Nvidia’s massive software ecosystem — compilers, libraries, debuggers, and frameworks built over 18 years — that locks developers into Nvidia hardware. It matters because even when competitors build competitive hardware, the cost of porting software keeps developers on Nvidia platforms.

How are AI coding agents threatening Nvidia’s CUDA dominance?

AI coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot can now write, port, and optimize GPU kernels autonomously. This dramatically reduces the engineering effort required to build software for non-Nvidia hardware, collapsing the cost advantage that CUDA’s ecosystem provided.

Can AI agents really port CUDA code to other platforms?

Yes. Concrete examples include Claude Code porting LeelaChessZero’s CUDA backend to AMD ROCm (January 2026) and Infinity using AI agents to recreate CUDA-like software for D-Matrix in 10 hours (August 2026). These are real, verified cases of AI agents crossing the CUDA moat.

What is AMD doing differently with ROCm.AI?

AMD published a machine-readable ISA so AI models can program directly to AMD hardware, and launched ROCm.AI — a suite of tools that integrates with existing code assistants to deploy, debug, and optimize for AMD Instinct GPUs. This represents a fundamentally new approach: instead of translating CUDA code, let AI agents write native code for AMD hardware.

Is Nvidia’s CUDA moat completely broken?

No. Nvidia still has the best hardware performance, the most mature software ecosystem, and deep relationships with AI researchers. The moat is eroding, not collapsing. However, the direction of travel is clear — AI coding agents are accelerating the pace at which competitors can build compatible software stacks, and the shift from training to inference reduces CUDA’s lock-in advantage.

item.title: Nvidia Vera CPU: Purpose-Built for Agentic AI Workloads — Full Review
item.description: Nvidia Vera CPU delivers 6x faster agentic AI performance than x86 with 88 Olympus cores, 1.2 TB/s memory bandwidth, and 40% lower latency.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — The Agentic AI CPU Moment

For the first time in the modern computing era, a CPU has been designed from the ground up specifically for agentic AI workloads rather than retrofitted for them. Nvidia Vera, powered by 88 custom Olympus cores based on the Armv9.2 architecture, delivers up to 6x faster agentic AI performance than AMD EPYC Turin (Zen 5), achieves 40% lower peak loaded latency than traditional x86 data center CPUs, and provides over 3x per-core memory bandwidth at less than half the power. Vera is not merely a faster server chip — it represents Nvidia’s strategic pivot from GPU-only supplier to full-stack AI infrastructure provider, and it may redefine how the industry thinks about the CPU’s role in AI factories.

What Is Nvidia Vera? — A Ground-Up Architecture for Agentic Workloads

Nvidia Vera is a custom Arm-based server processor built on the Olympus microarchitecture, announced in 2026 as the host CPU for Nvidia’s next-generation AI infrastructure. Unlike previous Nvidia server CPUs such as Grace (which paired Arm Neoverse cores with Hopper GPUs), Vera is a monolithic die design with 88 custom cores that Nvidia architected in-house specifically for the demands of agentic AI — code generation, tool calling, sandbox execution, reinforcement learning orchestration, and real-time context management.

The first Vera CPUs were hand-delivered by Nvidia VP Ian Buck to Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Oracle in May and June 2026, signaling that Nvidia is targeting the most demanding AI workloads from day one. Oracle Cloud became the first hyperscaler to commit to large-scale Vera deployment, planning hundreds of thousands of units starting in 2026.

88 Olympus Cores: Built for Branch-Heavy, Sequential AI Tasks

The Olympus core is the heart of Vera. Each core features a 64 KB instruction cache with 128 bytes/cycle fetch bandwidth and a 10-wide decode pipeline — significantly wider than both AMD Zen 5 and Intel’s latest architectures. This wide front-end is critical for agentic AI workloads, which are characterized by unpredictable branch patterns, frequent context switches, and serialized code execution.

Nvidia’s proprietary Spatial Multithreading technology allows each Olympus core to handle multiple threads with improved parallel execution efficiency compared to traditional simultaneous multithreading (SMT). The result is up to 1.9x IPC (instructions per cycle) uplift over AMD Zen 5, with branch prediction up to 2.3x faster and backend operations per cycle up to 4.3x faster than AMD’s latest architecture.

Metric Nvidia Olympus AMD Zen 5 Intel Granite Rapids
Core count 88 Up to 192 (chiplet) Up to 128 (chiplet)
ISA Armv9.2 x86-64 x86-64
Decode width 10-wide 6-wide 6-wide
IPC uplift vs Zen 5 Up to 1.9x Baseline ~1.1x
Branch prediction vs Zen 5 Up to 2.3x faster Baseline ~1.2x faster
Backend ops/cycle vs Zen 5 Up to 4.3x faster Baseline ~1.3x faster
Die design Monolithic Chiplet (CCD + IOD) Chiplet (compute + uncore)

Monolithic Die Design vs Chiplet x86: Why It Matters for AI

One of Vera’s most significant architectural decisions is its monolithic die design with adjacent dielets, in contrast to the chiplet-based approaches used by AMD EPYC (multiple CCDs connected via Infinity Fabric) and Intel Xeon (multiple compute tiles). Chiplet designs introduce NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) penalties — when a core needs to access data on a remote chiplet’s memory controller, latency increases significantly.

For agentic AI workloads, where every millisecond of latency compounds across thousands of sequential tool calls and LLM inference steps, NUMA penalties are not acceptable. Vera’s monolithic design ensures uniform memory access latency across all 88 cores, eliminating the performance variability that plagues chiplet x86 CPUs in latency-sensitive AI scenarios.

Key Specifications and Architecture Deep Dive

Olympus Core Microarchitecture (Armv9.2, FP8, Spatial Multithreading)

The Olympus core implements the Armv9.2 instruction set with Nvidia-specific extensions optimized for AI workloads. Key microarchitectural features include:

  • 10-wide decode pipeline — among the widest in any server CPU, enabling high instruction throughput for complex AI orchestration code
  • 64 KB L1 instruction cache with 128 bytes/cycle fetch — ensures the front-end never stalls on branch-heavy agent code
  • Native FP8 precision support — accelerates AI inference directly on the CPU without needing GPU offload for lightweight models
  • Spatial Multithreading — Nvidia’s proprietary threading technology that improves resource utilization compared to traditional SMT by dynamically allocating execution resources based on thread demand
  • Advanced branch prediction — 2.3x faster than AMD Zen 5, critical for the unpredictable control flow of agentic AI loops (tool selection, conditional branching, error handling)

Memory Subsystem: 1.2 TB/s LPDDR5X Bandwidth

Vera’s memory subsystem is arguably its most impressive specification. The CPU supports up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth via LPDDR5X SOCAMM modules, delivering approximately 14 GB/s per core. This is over 3x the per-core memory bandwidth of comparable x86 data center CPUs, achieved at less than half the power draw.

The high bandwidth is not just a benchmark number — it directly translates to real-world AI performance. Agentic AI workloads frequently involve loading and reloading large language model weights, KV caches, and sandbox state. With Vera’s memory bandwidth, these operations complete faster, reducing the CPU-side stalls that currently bottleneck GPU utilization in AI factories.

Memory Metric Nvidia Vera AMD EPYC Turin Intel Xeon Granite Rapids
Total bandwidth 1.2 TB/s ~600 GB/s ~500 GB/s
Per-core bandwidth ~14 GB/s ~3 GB/s ~4 GB/s
Memory type LPDDR5X SOCAMM DDR5 DDR5 / MCR DIMM
Power efficiency <50% of x86 Baseline Baseline
NUMA domains 1 (monolithic) 8-12 (chiplet) 4-8 (chiplet)

Scalable Coherency Fabric and NVLink-C2C Interconnect

Vera is not designed to operate in isolation. The Vera Rubin NVL72 system pairs Vera CPUs with next-generation Rubin GPUs via Nvidia’s NVLink-C2C interconnect, creating a tightly coupled CPU-GPU memory-coherent system. This means the CPU and GPU share a unified memory address space — data does not need to be copied between separate CPU and GPU memory pools, eliminating one of the most significant overheads in current AI infrastructure.

The scalable coherency fabric allows multiple Vera CPUs to be connected in a single system, supporting both single-socket and dual-socket configurations as well as liquid-cooled rack-scale deployments. For the largest deployments, Vera Rubin NVL72 racks integrate 72 Rubin GPUs with multiple Vera CPUs in a fully coherent, high-bandwidth fabric.

Performance Benchmarks: Vera vs x86 (AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon)

Agentic AI Workload Performance (6x faster, 40% lower latency)

In benchmark results published by Nvidia and independently verified by early adopters, Vera demonstrates dramatic performance advantages over x86 CPUs in agentic AI workloads. Against AMD EPYC Turin (Zen 5), Vera delivers up to 6x faster performance in end-to-end agentic AI tasks including code generation, repository querying, and multi-step tool orchestration.

The 40% reduction in peak loaded latency is particularly significant. In agentic AI systems, latency compounds across every step of the reasoning chain — each tool call, each LLM inference, each context window update. A 40% reduction at the CPU level translates to substantially faster end-to-end agent response times, directly impacting user experience and system throughput.

RL Training Throughput (85% vs 45% Evaluation Completion)

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and other RL-based training methods are central to modern AI model development. These workloads involve running thousands of evaluation episodes in parallel, each requiring CPU-based simulation, reward computation, and environment interaction.

Vera completes 85% of RL evaluations within the training window, compared to just 45% on baseline x86 CPUs. This near-doubling of evaluation throughput means AI labs can either train models faster with the same hardware or achieve higher quality results by running more evaluations within the same time budget. For organizations running RL at scale, this performance advantage directly translates to reduced training costs and faster iteration cycles.

IPC, Branch Prediction, and Memory Latency Comparisons

The architectural benchmarks paint a clear picture of Vera’s advantages:

  • IPC uplift: Up to 1.9x over AMD Zen 5, meaning each clock cycle accomplishes nearly twice the work
  • Branch prediction: 2.3x faster than Zen 5, critical for the unpredictable control flow of agentic AI
  • Backend operations per cycle: Up to 4.3x faster than Zen 5, reflecting the wider execution units and improved scheduling
  • Memory latency: Uniform across all cores due to monolithic design, eliminating the 20-40% latency penalty of cross-chiplet access in x86 CPUs

Why Agentic AI Needs a Different Kind of CPU

The CPU Bottleneck in AI Factories (Amdahl’s Law)

Amdahl’s Law states that the speedup of a system is limited by the portion of the workload that cannot be parallelized. In AI factories, GPUs handle the embarrassingly parallel matrix operations of neural network training and inference. But the serial portions — orchestration, tool calling, code interpretation, context management, and I/O coordination — run on CPUs.

As GPU performance has accelerated dramatically (Nvidia’s own GPUs have seen 1000x+ throughput improvements over the past decade), the CPU has become the bottleneck. A GPU may sit idle waiting for the CPU to prepare the next batch, manage KV caches, or coordinate multi-step agent workflows. Vera directly addresses this imbalance by providing CPU performance that can keep pace with modern GPU throughput.

Sandbox Execution, Tool Calling, and Code Interpretation

Agentic AI systems execute code in sandboxed environments, call external APIs, interpret results, and make decisions about next steps. These are fundamentally serial, branch-heavy workloads that do not benefit from GPU parallelism. Each step requires:

  1. Receiving the LLM’s output specifying a tool call
  2. Parsing and validating the call parameters
  3. Executing the tool (code compilation, API call, database query)
  4. Capturing and formatting the result
  5. Returning the result to the LLM for the next reasoning step

Vera’s 10-wide decode, superior branch prediction, and high per-core memory bandwidth make each of these steps faster. Nvidia reports up to 50% faster agentic sandbox performance and 4x sandbox density compared to x86-based racks, meaning a single Vera-based server can handle four times as many concurrent agent sessions.

KV-Cache Coordination and Context Management

Large language models maintain a KV (key-value) cache that stores the attention state of the current context window. In agentic AI systems, this cache must be frequently updated, swapped, and coordinated across multiple inference calls. The CPU is responsible for managing this cache — deciding what to keep, what to evict, and when to recompute.

Vera’s high memory bandwidth and low latency directly improve KV-cache management. With 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, cache evictions and reloads happen faster, reducing the time GPUs spend waiting for context to be ready. Nvidia’s benchmarks show that Vera minimizes CPU-side stalls and KV-cache eviction overhead, maximizing GPU utilization in mixed CPU-GPU AI pipelines.

Vera in the Ecosystem: Vera Rubin NVL72 and Beyond

Tightly Coupled CPU-GPU Architecture

Vera is the host processor for the Vera Rubin NVL72 system, which pairs Vera CPUs with next-generation Rubin GPUs via NVLink-C2C. This is not a traditional server architecture where CPU and GPU communicate over PCIe — NVLink-C2C provides a cache-coherent, high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnect that allows the CPU and GPU to share memory transparently.

The unified memory architecture eliminates the CPU-GPU data transfer overhead that currently consumes 20-30% of AI workload time. In traditional systems, data must be copied from CPU memory to GPU memory and back. With Vera and Rubin sharing a coherent memory space, pointers can be passed directly between CPU and GPU code without explicit data movement.

Oracle Cloud: First Hyperscale Deployment

Oracle Cloud is the first hyperscale cloud provider to commit to large-scale Vera deployment, planning to deploy hundreds of thousands of Vera CPUs starting in 2026. This is a significant strategic bet — Oracle is positioning its cloud as the premier platform for agentic AI workloads, leveraging Vera’s performance advantages to differentiate from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

For Oracle customers, this means access to AI infrastructure where the CPU is no longer the bottleneck. Agentic AI applications running on Oracle Cloud with Vera can expect faster response times, higher throughput, and better cost efficiency compared to x86-based alternatives.

Early Adopters: OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI

The list of early Vera adopters reads like a who’s who of AI industry leaders. OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceXAI all received first-generation Vera CPUs in mid-2026. These organizations run some of the most demanding agentic AI workloads in existence — from autonomous coding agents to large-scale RL training to AI-powered simulation.

Their adoption validates Nvidia’s thesis that agentic AI workloads have fundamentally different CPU requirements than traditional server workloads. If the organizations pushing the frontier of AI capabilities choose Vera over x86 alternatives, it signals a broader industry shift.

Market Impact: Nvidia vs AMD vs Intel in the AI CPU Era

Nvidia’s entry into the CPU market fundamentally changes the competitive landscape. AMD and Intel have dominated the server CPU market for decades, but neither has designed a chip specifically for agentic AI workloads. Their architectures are general-purpose, optimized for the broad range of enterprise workloads — databases, web servers, virtualization, and HPC.

Vera represents a specialized approach: a CPU optimized for a specific, rapidly growing workload class. This mirrors Nvidia’s strategy in the GPU market, where its CUDA ecosystem and specialized hardware (Tensor Cores, RT Cores) created an insurmountable lead over general-purpose GPUs from AMD and Intel.

Factor Nvidia Vera AMD EPYC Turin Intel Xeon Granite Rapids
AI-optimized design Yes (ground-up) No (general purpose) No (general purpose)
Agentic AI perf vs x86 Up to 6x faster Baseline ~1.2x faster
Memory bandwidth 1.2 TB/s ~600 GB/s ~500 GB/s
Power efficiency <50% of x86 Baseline Baseline
CPU-GPU coherence Native (NVLink-C2C) PCIe only PCIe only
Ecosystem lock-in Nvidia full stack Open ecosystem Open ecosystem
Availability Mid-2026 Current Current

The key question for data center operators is whether Vera’s performance advantages justify the ecosystem lock-in. Vera is designed to work optimally within Nvidia’s full-stack ecosystem — Vera Rubin NVL72, NVLink-C2C, CUDA, and Nvidia’s AI software stack. Organizations already invested in Nvidia’s ecosystem will find Vera a natural fit. Those running heterogeneous infrastructure may face integration challenges.

Conclusion — Is Vera the Future of AI Infrastructure?

Nvidia Vera represents a genuine architectural breakthrough for agentic AI workloads. The combination of 88 custom Olympus cores, 1.2 TB/s memory bandwidth, monolithic die design, and tight CPU-GPU integration via NVLink-C2C delivers performance that x86 CPUs simply cannot match for the specific demands of agentic AI.

However, Vera’s success depends on more than raw performance. The industry must decide whether the benefits of a specialized AI CPU outweigh the lock-in risks of a vertically integrated Nvidia stack. For AI labs and hyperscalers pushing the frontier of agentic AI — where every millisecond of latency and every watt of power matters — Vera’s advantages are compelling enough to justify the commitment.

The CPU bottleneck in AI factories is real, and Vera is the first product that directly addresses it. Whether it becomes the dominant AI CPU or a niche player in a still-diversifying market will depend on how quickly the rest of the industry responds. But one thing is clear: the era of the general-purpose CPU in AI data centers is ending, and the era of purpose-built AI CPUs has begun.

FAQ

What is the Nvidia Vera CPU?

The Nvidia Vera CPU is a custom Arm-based server processor built on the Olympus microarchitecture, designed specifically for agentic AI workloads. It features 88 custom cores, 1.2 TB/s of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth, and a monolithic die design that eliminates NUMA penalties common in chiplet-based x86 CPUs.

How much faster is Nvidia Vera than AMD EPYC for AI workloads?

Nvidia Vera delivers up to 6x faster performance in agentic AI workloads compared to AMD EPYC Turin (Zen 5). It also achieves 40% lower peak loaded latency and up to 1.9x IPC uplift over AMD’s latest architecture, with branch prediction up to 2.3x faster.

When will Nvidia Vera CPUs be available?

Nvidia began shipping Vera CPUs to early adopters including OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI, and Oracle in May-June 2026. Oracle Cloud plans to deploy hundreds of thousands of Vera CPUs starting in 2026, with broader availability expected through Nvidia’s partner ecosystem.

How does Vera’s memory bandwidth compare to x86 CPUs?

Vera delivers 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth via LPDDR5X SOCAMM modules, providing approximately 14 GB/s per core. This is over 3x the per-core memory bandwidth of comparable x86 data center CPUs, achieved at less than half the power consumption.

What is the Vera Rubin NVL72 system?

The Vera Rubin NVL72 is Nvidia’s next-generation AI infrastructure system that pairs Vera CPUs with Rubin GPUs via NVLink-C2C interconnect. It features a unified memory architecture where CPU and GPU share a coherent memory space, eliminating the data transfer overhead of traditional PCIe-based systems.

item.title: Commodification of Intelligence: Circular AI Deals and What They Mean for Costs
item.description: Circular AI deals — where AI companies invest in each other and commit to spending on each other's services — are reshaping how intelligence is priced and funded.
item.content:encoded:
Circular AI deals — where the same small group of hyperscalers, AI labs, and chipmakers invest in each other and simultaneously commit to spending billions on each other’s services — are transforming artificial intelligence from a speculative technology into a funded infrastructure asset class. These arrangements, which now total well over a trillion dollars in committed capital, are accelerating the commodification of intelligence itself, turning GPUs and data center capacity into fungible resources much like electricity, oil, or natural gas.

What Are Circular AI Deals? — A Simple Explanation

A circular AI deal occurs when Company A invests in Company B, and Company B simultaneously commits to spending a large portion of that investment on Company A’s products or services. The money flows in a loop rather than entering the broader economy. For example, Microsoft invests $13 billion in OpenAI, and OpenAI commits to spending $250 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform. The cash goes from Microsoft to OpenAI and then right back to Microsoft as cloud revenue.

This structure is not unique to AI. Japanese commodities trading houses (sogo shosha) have used similar circular financing arrangements since the 1960s to fund oil refineries, copper mines, and LNG terminals. The investor provides capital, and the recipient agrees to buy the investor’s infrastructure services — creating a guaranteed revenue stream that justifies the original investment.

What makes today’s AI circular deals different is their sheer scale. The amounts involved — hundreds of billions of dollars — are unprecedented outside of sovereign debt markets. And unlike traditional commodity infrastructure, the “product” being funded is intelligence itself: the compute power required to train and run the world’s most advanced AI models.

The Scale of Circular Deals in 2026

The numbers circulating in today’s AI ecosystem are staggering. Here is a breakdown of the major circular deals currently in place:

Amazon → Anthropic $5B (options for $20B more) Anthropic committed $100B+ to AWS Compute Forecast

Why Circular Deals Are Not Inherently Bad — The Commodity Infrastructure Analogy

It is tempting to label circular AI deals as fraudulent or as signs of a bubble. But the commodity infrastructure analogy suggests a more nuanced interpretation.

When a Japanese trading company finances a copper mine in Chile, it does so with a guaranteed offtake agreement: the mine’s output is pre-sold to the trading company’s industrial customers. The financing is secured against future production. The deal is circular in the sense that the financier is also the end customer, but it is rational because the underlying demand for copper is real.

The same logic applies to AI. Microsoft needs Azure to be the dominant cloud platform for AI workloads. OpenAI needs massive compute capacity to train increasingly capable models. A circular deal aligns both interests: Microsoft gets guaranteed Azure revenue, and OpenAI gets the compute it needs without having to raise all the capital upfront.

“These structures have been used in commodity markets for over 60 years,” notes Emerging Trajectories in their analysis. “GPUs and data centers are becoming fungible commodities, making circular deals rational and necessary.”

The key distinction is that commodity circular deals are backed by real end-user demand — people actually need copper, oil, and electricity. The question for AI is whether the end-user demand for intelligence services will grow fast enough to justify the committed infrastructure spending.

The Commodification of Intelligence: GPUs as Fungible Commodities

The circular deal phenomenon is both a cause and a consequence of the commodification of intelligence. As GPUs become standardized, interchangeable computing resources, and as data center capacity becomes a tradable asset, intelligence itself is being transformed from a bespoke service into a fungible utility.

Consider the trajectory of GPU pricing. In 2022, Nvidia H100 GPUs were scarce, allocation-controlled, and priced at a significant premium. By mid-2026, multiple GPU generations are available from Nvidia, AMD, and custom ASIC providers. Cloud GPU spot pricing has emerged, and secondary markets for compute credits are developing. This is the classic pattern of commodification: a scarce, differentiated product becomes a standardized, price-competitive commodity.

The implications for AI costs are profound:

  1. Compute costs are falling. As GPU supply expands and competition increases, the per-token cost of inference is dropping rapidly. What cost $10 per million tokens in 2024 may cost $0.10 by 2027.

  2. Intelligence becomes a utility. Just as businesses do not build their own power plants, they will increasingly not build their own AI infrastructure. They will buy intelligence by the token from hyperscaler cloud platforms.

  3. Circular deals accelerate commodification. By guaranteeing massive demand for compute, circular deals incentivize hyperscalers to build capacity at scale, which in turn drives down unit costs for everyone.

  4. The margin shifts from compute to data and distribution. When compute is a commodity, the competitive advantage shifts to who has the best data, the best distribution, and the best application-layer products.

The Real Risk: Valuation Inflation and the Untested Stress Test

While circular AI deals are structurally rational, they carry a specific and serious risk: valuation inflation based on committed spending from within a small circle, rather than genuine end-user demand.

Here is how the risk works. OpenAI reports $5 billion in annual revenue but $8.5 billion in annualized losses. Its valuation of $852 billion (from the March 2026 funding round) implies a price-to-revenue multiple of over 170x. A significant portion of OpenAI’s revenue comes from Microsoft Azure credits — which themselves originated from Microsoft’s investment in OpenAI. The circularity means that revenue and spending are partially endogenous to the system.

“If you strip out the circular revenue, what is the real end-user demand for OpenAI’s products?” asks Compute Forecast. “That is the question the market has not yet answered.”

The $785 billion in annual hyperscaler capex has never faced a demand moderation stress test. Since the AI boom began in late 2022, demand for AI compute has grown exponentially every quarter. But exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely. At some point, growth will moderate — and when it does, the circular deals that looked rational during the boom may reveal overcapacity and inflated commitments.

Compute Forecast identifies the core risk: “The risk is not collapse but inflated valuations based on committed spending from within a small circle.” In other words, the system is not necessarily fragile, but it may be significantly overvalued relative to genuine market demand.

The $250 Billion Question: Nvidia’s Ohio Backstop and What It Signals

The most dramatic circular deal to date is Nvidia’s reported discussion of a $250 billion backstop for OpenAI’s planned 10-gigawatt AI data center campus in Ohio, as reported by CNBC and the Wall Street Journal in July 2026.

To understand the scale: 10 gigawatts is enough to power approximately 8 million homes. It is more than the entire electricity consumption of some small countries. The data center campus would be the largest single electricity consumer in the United States.

Nvidia’s role as a backstop guarantor is significant because it represents a new level of entanglement. Nvidia is not just selling GPUs to OpenAI — it is guaranteeing the financing for the infrastructure that will house those GPUs. If OpenAI cannot pay its data center bills, Nvidia is on the hook for $250 billion.

This deal signals several things:

  • Nvidia’s confidence in long-term AI demand is extremely high. A $250 billion guarantee is not a casual bet.
  • The lines between chipmaker, cloud provider, and AI lab are completely blurred. Nvidia is now effectively a financier of AI infrastructure, not just a hardware supplier.
  • The scale of individual deals is growing faster than the underlying market. A $250 billion backstop for a single data center campus is unprecedented in any industry.

The Los Angeles Times reported on July 29, 2026, that Nvidia is working on fresh AI deals worth more than $750 billion in total. If even a fraction of these deals materialize, the circular AI deal market will exceed $2 trillion by the end of 2026.

Dot-Com Echoes vs. Genuine Demand — Two Views

The circular AI deal phenomenon has drawn comparisons to the dot-com bubble of 1999-2000. Jim Cramer, who lived through the dot-com era as a hedge fund manager, warned on CNBC on July 27, 2026: “I lived through 2000. I don’t want the sequel.”

Cramer’s concern centers on the circular financing structure. During the dot-com bubble, companies invested in each other, created reciprocal revenue arrangements, and inflated each other’s valuations. When the music stopped, the circularity collapsed, and so did the valuations. Nvidia’s shares fell more than 4% on the news of the Ohio backstop, suggesting that some investors share Cramer’s concern.

However, there are important differences between the dot-com era and today’s AI landscape:

The question is not whether AI has value — it clearly does — but whether the valuations and committed spending reflect that value or are inflated by circular financing.

What Happens If AI Demand Growth Moderates?

The most important scenario to consider is what happens when AI compute demand growth inevitably moderates from its current exponential trajectory.

In a demand moderation scenario:

  1. Hyperscalers face overcapacity. The $785 billion in annual capex was built for exponential growth. If growth drops to 30-40% annually, a significant portion of that capacity becomes surplus.

  2. Circular commitments become liabilities. OpenAI’s $250 billion Azure commitment, Anthropic’s $100 billion AWS commitment — these were negotiated when growth seemed infinite. If revenue growth slows, these commitments become crushing obligations.

  3. Backstop guarantors are tested. Nvidia’s $250 billion Ohio backstop would be called if OpenAI cannot pay. Even for a company with Nvidia’s market cap, a $250 billion loss would be devastating.

  4. The AI debt market amplifies losses. Emerging Trajectories warns of a potential multi-trillion-dollar AI debt market with mortgage-backed-security-like systemic risk emerging by 2029. If circular deals move off balance sheets into securitized debt products, a demand moderation could trigger a cascading financial crisis.

  5. Consolidation accelerates. Weaker AI labs and smaller cloud providers would be acquired or shut down. The circular deal structure favors incumbents who can afford to play the long game.

The most likely outcome is not a catastrophic collapse but a period of painful adjustment. Valuations would correct, some deals would be renegotiated, and the pace of infrastructure buildout would slow. The companies with genuine end-user demand and strong balance sheets — Microsoft, Amazon, Google — would emerge stronger. The question is which AI labs and chipmakers would survive the adjustment.

The Bottom Line for AI Costs and the Future of Intelligence Pricing

The commodification of intelligence, accelerated by circular AI deals, is driving a structural decline in the cost of AI compute. This is good news for businesses and consumers who use AI services. Lower compute costs mean cheaper API calls, more capable free-tier models, and broader AI adoption across the economy.

However, the circular deal structure introduces a layer of financial engineering that obscures the true cost of intelligence. When Microsoft books OpenAI’s Azure spending as revenue, and OpenAI counts Microsoft’s investment as capital, the system’s economics are not transparent. The real cost of intelligence — what end users actually pay — may be higher than it appears because the infrastructure costs are being subsidized by circular capital flows.

For businesses evaluating AI investments, the key takeaway is that AI costs will continue to fall in the medium term as compute commoditizes, but the financial system supporting AI infrastructure carries risks that could lead to price volatility in a downturn. The smart strategy is to build AI capabilities now, but avoid long-term lock-in contracts that assume today’s pricing and availability will persist indefinitely.

Intelligence is becoming a commodity. The question is not whether it will be cheap — it will be — but whether the financial infrastructure built to fund its creation can withstand the transition from exponential growth to sustainable maturity.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is a circular AI deal? A circular AI deal is an arrangement where one company invests in another, and the recipient commits to spending a significant portion of that investment on the investor’s products or services. For example, Microsoft invested $13 billion in OpenAI, and OpenAI committed to spending $250 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform, creating a circular flow of capital.

Are circular AI deals illegal or fraudulent? No, circular AI deals are not inherently illegal or fraudulent. Similar structures have been used in commodity infrastructure financing for decades, particularly by Japanese trading companies since the 1960s. However, they can create skewed incentives and obscure the true level of genuine end-user demand, which concerns some analysts and regulators.

How much money is involved in circular AI deals? The total committed capital in circular AI arrangements exceeds $1.5 trillion as of mid-2026. Major deals include Microsoft’s $13 billion investment in OpenAI paired with OpenAI’s $250 billion Azure commitment, Amazon’s $5 billion investment in Anthropic with Anthropic’s $100 billion AWS commitment, and Nvidia’s reported $250 billion backstop for OpenAI’s Ohio data center campus.

Could circular AI deals cause a financial crisis? Analysts at Emerging Trajectories warn that a potential multi-trillion-dollar AI debt market with mortgage-backed-security-like systemic risk could emerge by 2029. If circular deals move off balance sheets into securitized debt products and AI demand growth moderates, the resulting losses could cascade through the financial system. However, most current deals are on the balance sheets of well-capitalized companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and Nvidia, which limits systemic risk in the near term.

What does commodification of intelligence mean for AI pricing? Commodification means that AI compute — GPUs, data center capacity, and inference tokens — is becoming a standardized, fungible resource with falling prices. As GPU supply expands and competition increases, the per-token cost of AI inference is dropping rapidly. This makes AI more accessible to businesses and consumers but shifts competitive advantage from compute ownership to data, distribution, and application-layer innovation.
